title: Dual-Weighted Federated Learning for Battery Fault Diagnosis in Electric Vehicles
abstract: Dual-Weighted Federated Learning for Battery Fault Diagnosis in Electric Vehicles (FedWGT) : Source Code and Experimental Artifacts Overview This repository provides the source code and experimental artifacts for FedWGT, a coordinated federated dual-weighting framework for electric-vehicle battery fault diagnosis. FedWGT combines an effective-number-based class-balanced objective at vehicle clients with reliability-, data-volume-, and label-coverage-aware aggregation at the server. The implementation supports heterogeneous client partitions, auxiliary-inclusive and cell-signal-only input settings, matched federated baselines, demanding client conditions, component analysis, and client-side cell/block inspection-priority attribution. Contents The archive includes: • FedWGT client training and server aggregation implementations• MLSTM-FCN and comparison backbone implementations• FedAvg, FedProx, FedDyn, Trimmed-Mean, Multi-KRUM, pFedMe, and SCAFFOLD implementations• Fixed training, validation, and test definitions for the 96-cell and 98-cell cohorts• Configuration files for the reported experiment protocols• Drivers for the main benchmark and paired statistical analysis• Drivers for the 2×2 client-loss/server-aggregation component analysis• Long-horizon ratio-partition experiments• Demanding-client evaluations under stronger label skew, partial participation, and an increased client population• Client-side Integrated Gradients attribution analysis• Heterogeneity, adaptive server-optimizer, attribution, and statistical result files• Manuscript figures in PNG and PDF formats• Package-validation and unit-test scripts• SHA-256 checksums for distributed files Reproduction Create a Python environment and install the package: python -m venv .venvsource .venv/bin/activatepython -m pip install --upgrade pippython -m pip install -e . Validate the package and run the unit tests: python scripts/validate_package.pypython -m pytest -q Run the main benchmark and paired statistical analysis: python scripts/run_table9.py --data-root raw_data --device autopython scripts/summarize_tables9_10.py Run the client-loss/server-aggregation component analysis: python scripts/run_table11.py --data-root raw_data --device autopython scripts/summarize_table11.py The experiment drivers write newly generated outputs under the results/ directory. Detailed data placement, execution options, and output locations are provided in README.md. Data Raw battery measurements are distributed separately by the original data provider and are not redistributed in this archive. They can be obtained from the AI-Hub electric-vehicle battery dataset page: https://aihub.or.kr/aihubdata/data/view.do?dataSetSn=71347 After downloading the dataset, place the files under raw_data/ while preserving the relative layout referenced by data_splits/Dev_96 and data_splits/Dev_98. The included split definitions contain labels and relative paths but do not contain the raw battery measurement arrays. Software and Output Structure • fedwgt/: models, aggregation rules, data handling, and baseline implementations• scripts/: experiment, attribution, statistical-analysis, and validation programs• configs/: experiment configurations• data_splits/: fixed 96-cell and 98-cell cohort definitions• figures/: manuscript figures• results/: supplied experimental and statistical result files• tests/: unit tests for aggregation, attribution, and baseline regularization License The software is released under the MIT License. Please cite the associated article and this Zenodo record when using the implementation or supplied artifacts.

title: Stabilizer rank of the 8-qubit magic cat state: an exact rank-6 decomposition and calibrated evidence against rank 5
abstract: We report the stabilizer rank of the 8-qubit magic cat state |cat_8> (the magic-basis cat state of Qassim–Pashayan–Gosset, Quantum 5, 606 (2021)). Result. (i) Upper bound: chi(cat_8) <= 6, PROVEN exactly. An explicit rank-6 decomposition over 6-qubit-stabilizer-derived states is verified with sympy over Q(i): each candidate is checked to be a genuine stabilizer state by exact integer arithmetic (stabilizer group order exactly 2^n), target membership in the span is decided by exact rational rank, coefficients are produced exactly and the identity re-checked, and the whole decomposition is lifted back to 8 qubits and re-verified there. Reproduction: python3 verify.py ckpt_cat8_k6_cd.json (files bundled). (ii) Lower bound: chi(cat_8) >= 6, COMPUTATIONAL EVIDENCE, not a theorem. Two structurally independent searches over 5-tuples of stabilizer states — discrete pool coordinate descent (481 restarts, 30.9 core-hours) and continuous gradient descent with rounding (42 restarts, 1.99 core-hours) — both bottom out at 5-term residual 0.086664036 (9 hits each, never below, 523 restarts total) while both recover planted exact rank-5 witnesses at ~90% rate, calibrating the solvers against the exactness they fail to reach for cat_8. On this basis chi(cat_8)=6 is stated as a conjecture with a proven upper bound. Relation to Qassim–Pashayan–Gosset: their construction already implies chi(cat_8) <= 6; the present work adds the first explicit exact rank-6 decomposition of cat_8 and calibrated evidence against rank 5. The exponent log_2(6)/6 = 0.43083 does not improve their alpha = log_2(3)/4 = 0.39624; no published bound is improved and QPG's open questions remain open. The collapse-engine screen mandated by this machine's protocol was run on the continuation path (24-stage annealing path, one scale): read NULL (control -2.60 sigma = the flat-vector floor; permute gate ORDER-INVARIANT; counterfactual random walk reads identically). No claim in this record rests on it; the upper bound rests on the exact verification, the lower bound on search calibration. License: record CC-BY-4.0; bundled code additionally AGPL-3.0-or-later.

title: When Stories Evolve: Benchmarking LLM Storytelling Across Agent Architectures in Open-Ended World Simulations
abstract: Large language models can write fluent stories, but open-ended storytelling requires more than local fluency. In evolving world simulations and AI-native games, models must preserve facts, relationships, causal dependencies, and character states as the world changes. We introduce WSE-bench, a process benchmark that separately evaluates sustained generation, canonical coherence, and meaningful development in dynamic LLM storytelling. Generation Coverage records the proportion of planned narrative steps produced; Consistency tracks when canon breaks; and Richness measures how meaningfully branching, player-shaped trajectories develop. Across frontier models, Consistency and Richness do not form a smooth trade-off: their empirical Pareto frontier is non-concave, with several non-dominated intermediate configurations that no positive linear weighting can select. Added structure can enrich trajectories, but it does not uniformly improve coherence and may shorten them. Model scale chiefly improves sustained generation, without producing reliable gains in canonical coherence or meaningful development. These results show that sustained generation, canonical coherence, and meaningful development are distinct and sometimes competing capacities. WSE-bench makes those dynamics visible by extending narrative evaluation from finished stories to the processes that create them.

title: Computational Paradigm Explanation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Paradigm Explanation Theory (CPET), a new framework that integrates formal computational models, machine‑learning techniques, and philosophical insights to explain how and why novel computational methods lead to deep scientific principles. CPET posits a systematic mapping from a new computational method (New Method) to a corresponding deep principle (Deep Principle) and demonstrates that this mapping can serve as a basis for machine‑guided discovery of scientific theories. The theory is grounded in the idea that machine explanation provides a transparent, reproducible, and scalable mechanism for uncovering hidden regularities in data. We argue that CPET has the potential to be recognized by the Turing Award community because it offers a rigorous, generalizable, and theoretically rich approach to artificial intelligence that extends beyond pattern recognition to the generation of explanatory scientific knowledge.

title: Entropy-based Reduction Operator for Heuristic Binary Optimization
abstract: In this paper, we propose a reduction operator addressing discrete optimization problems, more precisely, for optimization problems with binary represented decisions. This operator may be integrated within various metaheuristics in order to reduce the dimension of the target problem. This is, by performing an iterative supervision over the browsed admissible space throughout the search process. We thus use the information entropy concept to measure the current uncertainty towards decision variables current values provided by an iterative heuristic search algorithm. Hence, it allows to explore the decision space more efficiently. Furthermore, we present two frameworks as effective applications of this operator: a pre-process for a hybrid approach and an interactive heuristic approach. We compare it against established approaches from the literature.

title: RDFdL: Integrating RDF with Differential Dynamic Logic
abstract: Knowledge graphs modeled in RDF are powerful for describing static knowledge, but they cannot capture or reason about the dynamic behavior of physical systems, e.g., systems described by differential equations, which is a critical gap for AI-driven cyber-physical systems. To solve this, we propose RDFdL, a framework that integrates RDF with Differential Dynamic Logic (dL) to represent and reason about both static knowledge and the continuous dynamics of physical systems. For the dynamic part, we syntactically represent differential equations and ranges in the state space in RDF and SHACL and provide semantics using a translation to dL. Linking RDF and dL through their shared foundation in first-order logic achieves a unique integration: verification results for safety and reachability properties in the dynamic logic domain become available as entailment to SPARQL queries over RDF data. We implement the pipeline using Apache Jena for ontology-driven RDF reasoning and KeYmaera X, the theorem prover for dL, and sketch its applicability in manufacturing.

title: A Cognitively Motivated Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Metaphor Explanations
abstract: Current evaluation of metaphor explanations relies mainly on holistic quality ratings, revealing little about how explanation quality is structured or where human judgments agree and diverge. We introduce a cognitively motivated framework that decomposes metaphor explanation quality into six theoretically grounded dimensions. In a dense annotation study (11,200 ratings), we find that: {\bfseries(i)} explanation quality is genuinely multidimensional; {\bfseries(ii)} annotator disagreement is systematic rather than random; and {\bfseries(iii)} the six dimensions collapse into a shared cluster and two independent axes of judgment. An exploratory feasibility study further shows that a standard automatic evaluation pipeline can recover parts of this structure, predicting the most discriminative dimensions well while its errors correlate human (dis)agreement. Together, these results suggest that multidimensional evaluation offers richer diagnostic insight than holistic ratings, and that automatic evaluators for open-ended generation tasks should be judged on how well they preserve the structure of human judgment.

title: TransDANN-Surv: When Domain-Adversarial Training (GRL/DANN) Fails in Cross-Population Cancer Survival Prediction
abstract: Large-scale mechanistic evidence that gradient-reversal domain-adversarial training (GRL/DANN) fails to improve cross-population cancer survival prediction: the distribution of cohort-level covariates (age, stage, event rate), of which missingness patterns are only the most visible surface, is the fundamental domain fingerprint. A domain classifier reaches 97-98% and cannot be suppressed by gradient reversal; controlled imputation (missingness to 0%) leaves it at 97.7%; and a leakage-free within-cohort imputation cannot fill fields that are structurally unobservable in a cohort. Input-level augmentation (mixup) is the only method surviving Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. This archive contains all analysis scripts, paper figures (Figures 1-8, S1-S5), and result tables (table1-19, Table S1-S7). Raw cohort data are not redistributed (TCGA, SEER, and cBioPortal license terms); they are reproducible via the documented download scripts.

title: Computational World Model Hierarchy Theory (CWMHT)
abstract: The Computational World Model Hierarchy Theory (CWMHT) proposes a unified framework for understanding how observations are transformed into abstract theories through a multi‑layered process. At its core lies a five‑step progression: Observation → Object → Event → Law → Theory. Each transition is governed by formal relationships that capture the essence of data abstraction, pattern extraction, causal inference, and symbolic representation. By articulating these relationships in a computationally tractable form, CWMHT bridges empirical data and theoretical knowledge, offering a pathway toward a generalized cognitive computing paradigm. This paper develops the theory, introduces its mathematical formulation, demonstrates its application across scientific domains, and discusses its potential to catalyze a Turing Award‑level breakthrough in unified cognition.

title: Adaptive Non-Playable Characters with Reinforcement Learning: Training and Shipping a Learned Game Opponent
abstract: Most Non-playable characters (NPCs) in modern video games still rely on scripted logic, finite state machines, and decision trees. This reliance on hand-authored rules means that their behaviour is easy to predict and repeat, which reduces player immersion and long-term engagement. Although reinforcement learning has been proposed as an alternative production method, prior demonstrations are often limited to experimental training environments and seldom implemented in a complete playable prototype. The present study fills this gap by taking a reinforcement-learning-trained NPC through the entire production pipeline, from initial design to a tested, standalone game capable of running on ordinary consumer hardware. We implemented a 3D foraging environment called the Flower Island in Unity, where we trained a hummingbird agent (with a 10-value observation vector, 5 continuous actions and a primary reward based on successful nectar collection) using Proximal Policy Optimization with the Unity ML-Agents toolkit and domain randomization applied throughout training. Training was run until the episodic cumulative reward, monitored in Tensor Board, showed progression from exploratory behaviour to more stable behavioural patterns, followed by a reward plateau, at which point the policy was exported for deployment. Once converged, the policy was exported in ONNX format and executed inside the finished game via Unity's Inference Engine on the Burst CPU backend; in playtesting the exported policy ran in real time without observed frame-rate degradation during playtesting and without inference-related runtime exceptions. This was part of a full title with two different game modes, a full user interface and layered audio system. The resultant policy showed purposeful and diverse foraging behaviour and was able to play against a human player in real time. The game passed all ten functional test cases, and the final acceptance test suite ran without any runtime exceptions. Among the engineering factors considered, integration effort, choice of inference backend, and simplicity of the reward structure exerted the greatest influence on the outcome. Formal quantitative benchmarking against a scripted baseline (reward curves, latency figures, and significance testing) was not captured for this iteration of the project and is identified as the primary direction for follow-up work. These results show that adaptive, learned NPCs are possible on commodity hardware and the pipeline described here provides a reproducible template for future games, simulations and educational tools.

title: Epistemic Drift in Recursive Model Training: Quantifying Tail-Knowledge Collapse in Synthetic Data Ecosystems
abstract: Abstract As AI-generated content increasingly saturates the open web, frontier models are progressively trained on data produced by earlier models rather than on purely human-authored sources. While the resulting phenomenon of model collapse, the recursive erosion of a model's output distribution toward its statistical center, has been demonstrated across language models, diffusion models, and Gaussian mixture models, little work has quantified its epistemic dimension: the disproportionate loss of rare, tail-distribution facts relative to common knowledge. This paper addresses that gap through a two-part computational simulation. The first experiment replicates the foundational Gaussian re-sampling collapse mechanism across 10 generations and 50 trials, confirming rising divergence from ground truth (KL divergence increasing 17.3-fold) alongside growing instability in variance estimation. The second experiment models a long-tailed (Zipfian) population of 1,000 discrete "facts" undergoing the same recursive training dynamic, isolating tail-specific knowledge loss. Results show that rare facts (the 900 lowest-frequency items) survive at a markedly lower rate (72.0% to 22.1%) than the corpus overall (74.8% to 28.5% support), with a statistically significant entropy decline (t(49) = -35.38, p < .001). These findings quantify, for the first time in this specific form, that recursive training does not degrade knowledge uniformly but strips out minority and specialist facts fastest, with direct implications for AI-assisted scientific, legal, and historical research. The paper concludes with recommendations for provenance tracking, data-accumulation strategies, and a proposed tail-survival benchmark for monitoring epistemic drift in production AI systems. Keywords: Model collapse; epistemic drift; synthetic data; recursive training; knowledge collapse; tail-distribution loss

title: Measuring Structured Predictability in Neural Training Dynamics: A Cross-Regime Study
abstract: Modern deep networks are trained through long update trajectories, yet their temporal organization remains less systematically characterized than architectures, losses, or optimizers. We study short-horizon predictability as a measure of temporal redundancy: where, when, and under which training conditions recent updates contain information about near-future parameter motion. We combine three complementary probe families, displacement-direction, subspace-residual, and predictor-based probes, with convention-aware, null-calibrated group-level readouts, and apply them to multi-pass vision training on CIFAR and public Pythia pretraining checkpoints. Across both regimes, vector-like tensors such as normalization parameters and biases (auxiliary parameters) exhibit simpler short-horizon dynamics than matrix-like feature-transforming weights (bulk parameters), whose predictable behavior concentrates in localized, time-varying pockets. Agreement within and across probe families, and with independent trajectory diagnostics, indicates that these measurements capture intrinsic trajectory structure, while probe differences distinguish complementary forms of temporal organization. Controlled CIFAR comparisons further show that architecture and training recipe systematically modulate the measured structure. A Pythia-70M case study further exposes a sequence of role-, depth-, and scale-dependent events, including bulk ESA falling below the random sign-agreement level and the emergence and redistribution of predictable qkv pockets across layers. These results position short-horizon predictability as a retrospective, parameter-resolved diagnostic of training dynamics.

title: Insurance Register Ontology (IRO)
abstract: An open OWL 2 ontology, SKOS registries, and SHACL governance layer for the authorization, cross-border operation, and identifier fabric of insurance and reinsurance undertakings, built and validated against the entire EEA register: 33,924 EIOPA register rows and 3,630 distinct LEI values, every one check-digit validated and cross-checked against a same-day GLEIF API harvest, joined into a 276,683-triple knowledge graph. The disagreements between the EU's own register of (re)insurers and the global LEI system are computed, graded and queryable, including a strict cross-register comparison against BaFin's published register. Code is MIT; ontology, SKOS registries, shapes and reports are CC BY 4.0.

title: The Bridge-Contract Criterion: A Form Audit for Transport Arguments, with an Instantiation in the abc Literature
abstract: The abc Gap Series: Part 2 — draft the contract DRAFT / work in progress. This is a versioned working paper of an ongoing research programme; newer versions supersede older ones. No claim about the truth of the abc conjecture, the correctness of IUT, or the correctness of the ATS series is made. Some proof claims resist line-by-line review not because individual steps are opaque, but because their load-bearing core is a transport: a quantity migrates between theoretical frameworks, and the claim's numerical content rests on the admissibility of that migration. A related class rests on global-only statements: assertions available only after summation over all places, with no place-wise access. This paper proposes a seven-component bridge contract and a versioned ledger audit. It reports a retrospective two-case feasibility illustration of the frozen v1-T transport ledger — the 1993 Fermat announcement as a retrospective known-gap case and an accepted volume-formula transport step as control — and one substantive selected-rows instantiation of the criterion in the abc literature, with a comparative discrimination case (the v1-F rows exercised there are named; the full-matrix coding of all rows is deferred). The paper contains no RH-side verdict; RH uniformity and global-only positivity claims are retained as an explicitly untested outlook. The criterion judges contract form, not mathematical truth: a served ledger is necessary, not sufficient, and the auditor tests the presence and addressability of an obligation, never its mathematical validity. Its value is that failures localize — the audit names the missing clause at a stated row instead of a diffuse doubt. ─────── ✦ ───────seriesdirectory (each part lists the whole series; planned parts are updated with title and DOI upon publication): ✔ Part 1: The Gap in IUTchIII, Corollary 3.12 — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19960781 (latest version) ☞ Part 2: The Bridge-Contract Criterion: A Form Audit for Transport Arguments, with an Instantiation in the abc Literature — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21960476 (latest version) ↳ Part 3: The Bridge Certificate — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21925803 (latest version) Part 4: The Bridge Certificate Applied to the Joshi ATS Series: A Ledger Audit — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21951155 (latest version) Part 5: The Joshi ATS Series under the Bridge-Certificate Standard: A Targeted Substance Audit and an All-Place Rigidity Classification of Effective Normalization Weights — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21956398 (latest version) Part 6: Repairing the ATS Chain? A Rigidity Theorem for Product-Formula Weights and an Effective-Weight Test for the Height Subchain — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21952486 (latest version) ↳ coming soon - Part 7: The bridge certificate applied to our own programme (self-application; working title) — (planned; appears in sync with the landscape paper) ✎ Tool supplement: The Global Normalization Contract Lemma — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21924253 (latest version) ℹ Companion (meta) paper: From Landscape to Atlas: Multi-Route Cartography of an Ongoing Expedition Toward the abc Conjecture (formerly: The abc Landscape) — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21916900 (latest version). The atlas paper is the complete memory of all routes; the series parts and capsule papers present selected results as independently citable units.

title: Adaptive Error Budget Allocation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Resource Estimation: A Metaheuristic Approach
abstract: System-level resource estimation is a key component of fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) toolchains. Its efficiency depends on how global error tolerance is allocated across logical operations, T-state distillation, and rotation synthesis to minimize physical resource overhead. The commonly used uniform-allocation strategy ignores circuit-specific structure and can overprovision inactive or less critical subsystems, leading to inflated space-time estimates. Prior work aims to address this limitation using supervised models trained on offline-generated datasets. However, this approach incurs additional data-generation costs and limits deployment flexibility. To overcome these drawbacks, we propose a training-free optimization framework that performs derivative-free search directly on the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator (AQRE), enabling instance-specific error budget allocation for previously unseen circuits without requiring offline training data. To evaluate robustness to optimizer choice, we instantiate the framework with two structurally distinct metaheuristics, simulated annealing and quantum particle swarm optimization. We evaluate our framework across 433 circuits spanning 2 to 91 qubits from 31 families in the MQT Bench suite. Across the benchmark suite, both methods reduce space-time cost by more than 33\% on average and agree within 1.34\% points, indicating that the gains are stable across different metaheuristic search strategies. Our analysis further finds that the optimization benefit is driven primarily by error-profile asymmetry rather than circuit scale, and the metric, Gini coefficient of optimized allocation, provides an interpretable diagnostic of expected improvement. Together, these results position adaptive error budget allocation as a system-software optimization layer for FTQC resource estimation pipeline.

title: Classical Verification of Quantum Advantage via Clifford Obfuscation
abstract: Demonstrating quantum advantage in a manner that can be independently verified by classical means remains one of the most pressing open problems in quantum computing. Here we propose a new heuristic approach for constructing quantum circuits that are hard to classically simulate yet whose output distributions can be efficiently verified classically. Our approach is based on Clifford circuit obfuscation. This obfuscation scheme hides the Clifford structure and injects a controlled and rapidly growing non-stabilizer resources that resist known classical attack strategies including reverse engineering and direct simulation. Our protocol is heuristic but is supported by both numerical and theoretical evidence. evidence.title: Classical Verification of Quantum Advantage via Clifford Obfuscation
evidence.abstract: Demonstrating quantum advantage in a manner that can be independently verified by classical means remains one of the most pressing open problems in quantum computing. Here we propose a new heuristic approach for constructing quantum circuits that are hard to classically simulate yet whose output distributions can be efficiently verified classically. Our approach is based on Clifford circuit obfuscation. This obfuscation scheme hides the Clifford structure and injects a controlled and rapidly growing non-stabilizer resources that resist known classical attack strategies including reverse engineering and direct simulation. Our protocol is heuristic but is supported by both numerical and theoretical evidence. This work provides a new avenue toward classically verifiable quantum advantage that avoids the stringent implementation requirements of known approaches.

title: المعايير الأساسية للتفسير الصحيح للنصوص – النصوص القانونية، على سبيل المثال
abstract: تتناول هذه الدراسة دور اللسانيات الجنائية (Forensic Linguistics) في تقييم النصوص القانونية والقضائية وتفسيرها. حيث تُوضّح أن النص القانوني لا يقتصر على القوانين والتشريعات الرسمية فحسب، بل يشمل أيضاً جميع المحاضر، والإفادات، والتقارير القضائية. واستناداً إلى المنهج الوصفي التحليلي، تم تصنيف النصوص وفقاً للجنس الأدبي/النمط (Genre)، وأسلوب الخطاب (Register)، وطبيعة الكتابة، مع تحديد أنواع النصوص القانونية وطرح أم نماذج وتحليلات متعلقة بالاستراتيجيات اللغوية. وأظهرت النتائج أن فحص جميع المستويات والمجالات اللغوية مجتمعةً يساهم في الكشف عن "البصمة اللغوية"، والتي تُعد أداة حاسمة لتحديد الهوية الحقيقية للمتحدث أو الكاتب في الجرائم اللغوية. فضلاً عن ذلك، فإن التوثيق الدقيق للغة المنطوقة كما هي يُحافظ على النية الإجرامية بشكل صحيح. لا تُعدّ اللغة في القطاعين القانوني والقضائي مجرد وسيلة للتواصل، بل هي أداة حاسمة في تحديد الحقوق والمسؤوليات الجنائية. يوفر علم اللغة الجنائية منهجًا علميًا لتحليل وتفسير النصوص المكتوبة والمنطوقة. وخلال عملية التقاضي، تواجه النصوص القانونية العديد من المشكلات، مثل تعدد المعاني. تكمن أهمية هذا البحث في أنه يُنشئ رابطًا علميًا بين اللغويات والقضاء. وسيساعد هذا العمل القضاة والباحثين والمشرعين على تجاوز التفسيرات السطحية من خلال الأدوات العلمية، كما سيوفر وضوحًا للمؤسسات الأكاديمية لدمج هذين المجالين في مناهجها الدراسية. فرضيات الدراسة: الفرضية الأولى: يمنع استخدام الأساليب والمعايير العلمية للتحليل اللغوي التفسيرات الذاتية والمضللة للنصوص القانونية. الفرضية الثانية: يُسهم الحفاظ على اللغة المنطوقة العفوية في الشهادات (دون تعديل ثقافي) في تحديد البصمة اللغوية للمتحدث، ويساعد في تحديد النية الإجرامية.

title: sequoia-boost
abstract: sequoia-boost is a pure Rust implementation of gradient boosted decision trees modeled on the public algorithms and interfaces of XGBoost. It provides exact, histogram, and approximate tree construction, regularized second order optimization, DART and linear boosters, multiclass classification, regression, count models, ranking objectives, categorical features, missing value handling, monotone constraints, and feature interaction constraints. Trained models support early stopping, cross validation, feature importance, leaf prediction, TreeSHAP contributions, and TreeSHAP interaction values. Data can be constructed from dense or sparse matrices and loaded from CSV or libsvm files. Models can be stored in native binary or JSON formats. Numeric tree ensembles can also be imported from or exported to XGBoost JSON, while unsupported DART, linear, and categorical exports return errors. The crate is intended for Rust applications that need gradient boosting without C or C++ linkage. It requires Rust 1.86 or newer and uses Rayon for parallel CPU histogram construction. Tests cover deterministic behavior, serialization, model quality, and selected compatibility with upstream XGBoost.

title: GPT-EBD2N training logs
abstract: Four complete training records, one per model size of the scaling table, each the concatenation of the SLURM job logs of the run in chronological order (a ########## job ########## line opens each slice). Every slice resumes exactly where the previous one stopped, at the epoch boundary, with the optimizer and learning-rate schedule restored, so the files show the whole trajectory: configuration, placement, per-epoch throughput and memory, validation accuracy after each epoch, checkpoint writes. ebd2n_254M_training.out — 254 M, MiniPile, 4× H200, 5 epochs, jobs 2249572 + 2255117; validation 47.2 → 52.0 %. ebd2n_483M_training.out — 483 M, 4× H200, jobs 2649838 → 2649840 → 2649839 (two epochs per slice); 54.2 % after 6 epochs (the table stops at epoch 5, same budget as the other sizes). ebd2n_778M_training.out — 778 M, jobs 2656856, 2674201, 2708786, 2718872, 2723380, 2764684 (one epoch per slice); 54.9 % after 6 epochs. ebd2n_1410M_training.out — 1.41 B, 8× H200, pipeline depth 3, jobs 3132735, 3133145, 3133146, 3133147, 3133148 (one epoch per 24 h slice); 49.6 → 55.5 % over 5 epochs. Run dashboard — [run tag]_[job id].html Self-contained HTML report written by the EBD2N runtime at the end of a training run. Opens in any browser offline; [run tag]_[job id].json holds the same data. It records, from the training process itself: the run identity (purpose, configuration, command line, host, GPUs, PyTorch/CUDA versions, git commit [commit]); the hyper-parameters (model, optimisation, numerics, pipeline depth, freeze and LoRA recipe); the final metrics (validation accuracy per epoch, loss and token accuracy per batch, throughput, peak memory per GPU, trainable parameters); interactive curves with a table view; and, for every unit, its device, state (frozen / LoRA / full rank), parameters, optimizer steps taken and skipped. Scores computed afterwards from the saved checkpoint appear in the job log, not here. Generated by ebd2n/report.py, included with its test in the code archive.

title: Learning Auditable Classifier Models: Source-Disjoint Tree Ensembles
abstract: Predictive models in clinical and regulated settings must be accurate and fully auditable. Tree ensembles deliver strong accuracy on tabular data, but their sequential boosting couples structure discovery with coefficient estimation, making compact per-prediction auditing difficult. Interpretable alternatives impose structural constraints that limit expressiveness: generalized additive models typically restrict interactions to pairwise terms and post-hoc rule extractors produce overlapping rules that hinder compact interpretation. We introduce Residual Pattern Tree Ensemble (RPTE), a three-stage learning approach, that is built on three key principles: bounded feature budget, source disjointness, and separate coefficient estimation. Stage~1 builds a supervised symbolic feature vocabulary. Stage~2 grows shallow trees under a source-disjointness constraint, where each raw variable is allocated to at most one tree, and retains only the discovered tree structures. Stage~3 solves a single $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression over leaf-region indicators, yielding jointly optimal sparse coefficients. This learning approach ensures that every prediction decomposes into an algebraic sum of named, non-overlapping rule contributions, enabling full auditability by design. Empirical evaluation on twelve clinical-domain binary classification benchmarks using repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation shows that RPTE performs competitively against tuned opaque ensembles and interpretable baselines. RPTE reduces model inspection units by 9$\times$ to 87$\times$ relative to XGBoost and maintains lower audit complexity than EBM on all 12 datasets. RuleFit requires comparable or fewer inspection units on three datasets where its rule count is small, but without source-disjointness guarantees. The source code is available at \href{https://github.com/srikumar2050/hugiml-core}{this https URL}.

title: Proceedings of the second international workshop on AI systems for the environment 2026 (AISE 2026)
abstract: Welcome to the second edition of AISE, the International Workshop on AI Systems for the Environment. AISE brings together researchers working at the intersection of artificial intelligence and environmental sustainability, with the aim of exploring how AI methods can support more effective and responsible decision-making in complex sustainability domains. Building on the first edition of the workshop, held at ECAI 2025 in Bologna, AISE 2026 provides a focused forum for methodological advances and application-driven research addressing pressing environmental challenges. Tackling sustainability challenges such as renewable energy management, biodiversity conservation, circular economy design, sustainable agriculture, transportation, and reducing AI's own environmental footprint requires methods that can operate effectively in complex and interconnected settings. AISE therefore welcomes research spanning a broad range of AI areas, including machine learning, optimisation, reinforcement learning, multiagent systems, agent-based modelling, explainable AI, human-in-the-loop methods, and intelligent decision support. The papers accepted to AISE 2026 reflect this breadth. The first group of contributions are focused on environmental monitoring, agriculture, and the circular economy, addressing topics including the detection of illegal wildlife trade, interpretable crop management, cold hardiness prediction, bulky waste material classification, and explainable urban mining. The second group focuses on sustainable optimisation and intelligent energy systems, with contributions on multiagent reinforcement learning for battery management, optimisation for irregular packing, and multiagent AI for power grid studies. The workshop also features a keynote by Dr. Hendrik Baier on explainable AI for sequential decision making and its role in sustainable mobility. His talk highlights an important challenge for sustainability-oriented AI that ``\textit{technically effective optimisation and planning methods will have limited real-world impact if their recommendations cannot be understood, discussed, refined, and trusted by the people expected to use them}''. This perspective complements the broader aims of AISE by connecting optimisation, explainability, human-AI interaction, and sustainability-oriented decision making. We hope these proceedings provide a useful snapshot of current research on AI systems for environmental sustainability and foster further collaboration across artificial intelligence, optimisation, multiagent systems, environmental science, energy systems, agriculture, mobility, and circular economy research. We thank all authors, reviewers, organisers, session chairs, and participants for contributing to AISE 2026 and to the continuing development of the AISE community. Further details about AISE 2026 are available on the workshop webpage: https://sites.google.com/view/aise2026

title: Computational Self-Explanation Theory (CSET-2): A Formal Framework for Transparent Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Computational Self-Explanation Theory (CSET-2) proposes a principled approach to demystifying the decision‑making processes of complex artificial systems. By treating each inference as a node in a directed graph and enforcing a bidirectional mapping between observable outputs and internal rationales, CSET-2 establishes a rigorous protocol for generating self‑explanatory traces. The theory extends traditional self‑explanation from human cognition to computational agents, offering formal definitions, algorithmic procedures, and complexity analyses. This paper presents the core concepts of CSET-2, derives its formal representation, outlines an implementation strategy, and discusses potential applications in explainable AI, autonomous robotics, and human‑machine interaction. The framework is designed to satisfy Turing Award‑level criteria for interpretability, providing a scalable solution for breaking AI black boxes.

title: Computational Personality Explanation Theory
abstract: Computational Personality Explanation Theory (CPET) proposes a unified computational framework that links observable behavior, underlying personality traits, and the causal reasons that drive both. By formalizing the triadic relationship Behavior → Personality → Reason, CPET aims to explain why a system exhibits a particular behavioral style, rather than merely predicting that style. The theory introduces a probabilistic generative model that decomposes behavior into latent personality dimensions and interprets these dimensions through a hierarchy of explanatory factors. This paper outlines the core mathematical constructs of CPET, demonstrates how it can be instantiated for agent-based systems, and discusses its implications for enhancing interpretability in artificial intelligence. The resulting framework not only provides a principled way to generate explanations but also offers a path toward Turing Award‑level contributions by elevating the explainability of intelligent agents.

title: Proof Path Compression Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Proof Path Compression Theory (PPCT), a novel approach to simplifying complex proof investigations. The core concept revolves around identifying and eliminating redundant paths within a proof process. We postulate the existence of a significant amount of superfluous pathing, represented as: [ P = {p_1, p_2, ..., p_K} ] where 'p_i' represents a specific path within the proof. The theory then focuses on determining the shortest core path, which, upon identification, allows for a streamlined and efficient resolution of the original problem. This methodology offers potential improvements in the study of intricate proofs by reducing unnecessary computational steps and focusing analytical efforts on the most critical aspects of the argument. The presented framework prioritizes direct path minimization, a key element in achieving efficient proof reduction. ---

title: Do Language Models Consistently Encode the Current Year?
abstract: A consistent concept of the current time is important for temporal reasoning, yet how language models represent the current time is not well understood. We contribute two tasks that probe the current year in conceptually distinct ways: an associative task, which infers the current year from verb tense, and a declarative task, which directly queries for the current year. Both tasks estimate current years within one year of the post-training data cutoff of instruction-tuned language models. For base models, predictions on the associative task serve as a strong proxy for the pre-training data cutoff, with an average error of only 10 months across 13 models. However, their internal mechanisms diverge: the associative task uses mechanisms similar to factual recall, while the declarative task lacks consistent causal pathways. This divergence poses a challenge for updating the current year in language models. None of prompting, SFT, or weight editing succeed in shifting the associative and declarative years simultaneously. evidence.abstract: A consistent concept of the current time is important for temporal reasoning, yet how language models represent the current time is not well understood. title: Computational Proof Verification Generation Theory (CPVGT)
abstract: The rapid growth of automated theorem proving and symbolic reasoning systems has created a pressing need for mechanisms that can simultaneously generate mathematical proofs and verify their correctness in an integrated manner. This paper introduces the Computational Proof Verification Generation Theory (CPVGT), a novel framework that unifies proof construction and verification within a single computational pipeline. CPVGT is built upon a modular architecture that couples a proof generator with a verifier component, forming a coherent structure denoted as [Proof + Verifier]. By leveraging recent advances in deep learning, symbolic manipulation, and formal logic, CPVGT demonstrates a scalable approach to proof discovery that inherently guarantees validity. The theoretical foundations of CPVGT are explored through formal definitions, algorithmic descriptions, and complexity analyses, highlighting its potential to bridge artificial intelligence and formal mathematics. The paper discusses practical applications, including automated proof synthesis for complex conjectures and educational tools for learning mathematical reasoning. While no experimental data is presented, the theoretical results suggest that CPVGT could serve as a cornerstone for future research aimed at achieving a unified proof ecosystem.

title: Computational Personality Formation Theory (CPFT)
abstract: Computational Personality Formation Theory (CPFT) proposes a principled framework for understanding how autonomous computational systems develop stable, long‑term behavioral traits through continuous interaction with their environment. The central hypothesis of CPFT is that personality emerges from the transformation of raw interaction data into internal patterns, which in turn shape the system's future responses. This paper formalizes the Interaction → Pattern → Personality (IPP) chain, distinguishes personality from conventional model parameters, and outlines the mathematical mechanisms that underpin personality formation. We argue that CPFT offers a scalable foundation for personalized artificial intelligence, with potential implications for the next generation of adaptive agents and the broader field of AI individuality.

title: Computational Causal Reconstruction Theory (CCRT)
abstract: The field of causal inference has traditionally focused on identifying cause–effect relationships from observational data, often relying on assumptions about the data generation process. Computational Causal Reconstruction Theory (CCRT) proposes a complementary perspective: given an observed output of a complex system, we seek to reconstruct the hidden computational causes that produced it. CCRT formalizes this reverse engineering problem within a probabilistic framework, linking outputs to latent computational structures through a mapping that can be learned or inferred. By treating the system as a black box that implements an unknown algorithm, CCRT provides a principled method to recover the underlying computation from input–output traces. This paper develops the theoretical foundation of CCRT, presents inference algorithms, discusses identifiability conditions, and illustrates potential applications in understanding deep neural networks, biological signaling pathways, and engineered digital circuits. The theory has implications for both interpretability and robustness in AI systems and offers a new lens for exploring the computational nature of complex phenomena.

title: Bidirectional Proof Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Bidirectional Proof Theory (BPT), a novel approach to logical proof construction. Traditional proof systems rely on a unidirectional flow, demonstrating implication (A → B). BPT shifts this paradigm by simultaneously examining bidirectional relationships (A ↔ B), aiming to identify and leverage the shortest, most structurally efficient paths between statements. The core of BPT lies in the search for dual-directional structures that represent a balanced and interconnected set of logical assertions. This approach promises to fundamentally alter the way proofs are constructed, potentially leading to more concise, robust, and adaptable proof systems. The presented theory outlines the foundational concepts, operational rules, and potential applications of BPT.

title: Few-Shot Cross-Dataset Adaptation for Tuberculosis Detection Using DenseNet
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) is one of the most common and dangerous bacterial ailments. Every year, it causes a large number of deaths worldwide. Although many deep learning models can detect tuberculosis from chest X-rays quite accurately, severe domain shift across datasets makes the task challenging. Different imaging protocols, patient demographics, and equipment across domains make the task of generalization difficult. In real-world settings, a model may perform well on one dataset but show a noticeable drop in performance when tested on another. In this work, we address this domain adaptation challenge through a few-shot scaling study. A controlled cross-dataset evaluation is presented in this paper using TBX11K as the source domain and the Mendeley TB dataset as the target domain. It is investigated how varying the number of target samples affects model performance under three training regimes: frozen backbone adaptation, full fine-tuning of a source-pretrained DenseNet121 model, and training from scratch. The results indicate that the model can perform well even with limited data and can achieve 98.36\% accuracy with just 75 labeled samples per class. The adaptation curves demonstrate how fine-tuning effectively mitigates domain shift. These findings establish full fine-tuning of pretrained models as a highly effective and practical strategy for mitigating domain shift in low-resource clinical deployment scenarios.

title: A minimal qutrit counterexample to Conjecture 4.9 of Lesniewski and Ruskai
abstract: Lesniewski and Ruskai conjectured that the contraction coefficient of every monotone Riemannian metric under a unital stochastic map equals the Hilbert--Schmidt contraction on the traceless subspace. We disprove the conjecture with an explicit entanglement-breaking qutrit channel induced by a doubly stochastic $3\times3$ matrix. A faithful diagonal state and a commuting traceless tangent give, simultaneously for every normalized monotone metric, the exact lower bound $η^{\mathrm{Riem}}_κ(Φ_K)\ge 8896/20007>(62+2\sqrt{61})/225=Λ_2(Φ_K^{\dagger}Φ_K)$. The counterexample is entirely classical on a maximal abelian subalgebra. A theorem of Hiai and Ruskai establishes the conjectured identity for all unital qubit maps, so dimension three is minimal among full matrix algebras.

title: Computational Language Explanation Theory (CLET-2)
abstract: The present work introduces Computational Language Explanation Theory (CLET‑2), a formal framework that bridges the gap between syntactic representations generated by artificial intelligence systems and their semantic interpretations. CLET‑2 posits that every machine‑produced language artifact should be accompanied by an explanatory mapping that justifies its effectiveness and meaning. By formalizing this mapping as a function Language→Meaning, the theory provides a systematic method for validating AI‑generated code, natural language outputs, and other computational artifacts. The theoretical foundation draws from formal language theory, semantics, and algorithmic information theory. It further proposes algorithmic procedures that can be integrated into existing AI pipelines, enabling real‑time explanation generation without sacrificing performance. The potential impact of CLET‑2 includes heightened transparency, improved debugging capabilities, and a pathway toward Turing‑award worthy systems that produce self‑explanatory, trustworthy software. The paper details the core concepts, formal definitions, algorithmic implementations, and discusses open research directions.

title: Geometric Flow Theory of Proofs (GFTP)
abstract: This paper introduces Geometric Flow Theory of Proofs (GFTP), a novel approach to proof manipulation and optimization based on the continuous deformation of proofs. The core idea posits that proofs, analogous to physical objects, can undergo continuous transformations. GFTP seeks to identify pathways where complex proofs evolve into simpler ones, effectively navigating from challenging to more tractable states. This is achieved through a geometric framework where proofs are represented as continuous functions and subject to flow equations. The theory's potential lies in its ability to provide a systematic method for proof optimization and potentially unlock new strategies in mathematical reasoning and verification. This document outlines the fundamental concepts, key formulas, and the theoretical underpinnings of GFTP. ---

title: Perbandingan Kinerja Algoritma Cheng and Church dan Qualitative Biclustering pada Data Produksi Perikanan Budidaya Indonesia
abstract: Biclustering is a two-dimensional clustering approach that simultaneously identifies relationships between objects and variables, making it more suitable than conventional clustering methods for analyzing data with local patterns. Although numerous biclustering algorithms have been developed, comparative studies evaluating their performance on official statistical data remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of the Cheng and Church (CC) and Qualitative Biclustering (QUBIC) algorithms using Indonesia’s aquaculture production data for 2023. The dataset comprised the production of 14 aquaculture commodities across 34 provinces. Optimal parameters for both algorithms were determined through a manual tuning procedure. Their performance was subsequently evaluated using the Mean Squared Residue (MSR), Average Squared Residue (ASR), and the Liu–Wang index. The results showed that the optimal parameter for the CC algorithm was δ = 0.009, while the optimal QUBIC parameters were r = 1, q = 0.06, and c = 0.75. CC produced 7 biclusters with an ASR of 0.0052, whereas QUBIC produced 8 biclusters with an ASR of 0.4360. The lower MSR and ASR values of CC compared with QUBIC indicate that CC was more effective in forming homogeneous biclusters in aquaculture production data. The number of province memberships showed that both algorithms were able to capture patterns across most provinces, although CC had slightly broader coverage. The Liu and Wang index value of 0.1951 indicated a relatively low similarity between the bicluster membership structures produced by CC and QUBIC. Thus, although both algorithms were applied to the same aquaculture production data, CC and QUBIC tended to produce different clustering structures.

title: Reset-Locked Compliance: Session Boundaries, Not Held Constraint, in Governed Language Agents
abstract: A governed language agent's rule-following may not be a property it holds, but a property it recovers at each session reset and loses across the turns that follow. If true, obedience is locked to the session boundary rather than held independently of it, predicting a repeating shape: high compliance early in a session, falling compliance later, restored again when a new session opens under the same governing contract. This study tests that prediction using the turn-level compliance record produced by the Continuity Governance Mesh, comparing compliance across sessions at matched within-session positions so that only the number of intervening resets differs. The chance distribution of the pattern is derived in advance, and a result is reported as reset-locking only if the observed pattern exceeds it at a threshold fixed before any data is examined. A finding of no difference is reported with equal completeness, since the field currently has evidence in neither direction.

title: Harmonic higher weight distributions, Simonis' approach of MacWilliams identity and moments
abstract: We present a combinatorial proof of Simonis type MacWilliams identity for harmonic higher weight distributions of linear codes. Furthermore, we investigate the statistical moments of the harmonic higher weight enumerators for random linear codes. Defining the enumerators via rank functions of the generator matrices of linear codes, we prove that its expectation vanishes for all non-trivial harmonic functions due to the inherent symmetry of random matrices, and we also derive an explicit, non-trivial formula for the covariance.

title: Computational Representation Discovery Algorithm (CRDA)
abstract: The explosive growth of data in modern science and industry has created an urgent need for automated methods that can discover new representations of raw information. Existing representation learning methods, such as autoencoders and variational inference, largely depend on human‑designed architectures and loss functions, which limits their ability to uncover unforeseen structural regularities in data. In this paper, we propose the Computational Representation Discovery Algorithm (CRDA), a principled framework that takes as input a large corpus of data and a set of tasks, and outputs a new representation structure that maximizes task performance while preserving data fidelity. CRDA is formulated as an optimization problem over the space of possible representation graphs, where nodes correspond to latent concepts and edges encode semantic relationships. By leveraging graph‑based evolutionary search, constraint‑driven gradient updates, and a novel representation fidelity metric, CRDA autonomously generates hierarchical, interpretable representations that can be reused across diverse downstream applications. We provide a detailed theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence properties and computational complexity, and we discuss its potential to revolutionize data science by enabling machines to create new scientific knowledge. The algorithm's capacity to discover representations that are both compact and highly predictive positions it as a strong candidate for future Turing Award recognition.

title: Information Conservation Flow Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Information Conservation Flow Theory (ICFT), a novel framework centered on the concept of information flow within mathematical transformations. The core principle posits that information, represented as I(X), transforms when a mathematical operation is applied, leading to I(Y). The theory aims to identify and establish conservation laws governing these transformations, potentially leading to the discovery of new information invariants. ICFT suggests a fundamental shift in how we perceive mathematical operations, moving beyond mere functional changes to recognize the persistent nature of information itself. This work lays the groundwork for exploring the implications of ICFT across various mathematical domains, with the goal of uncovering previously unseen conservation laws and ultimately, novel mathematical constructs. ---

title: Stable Flow Theory of Proofs
abstract: This paper introduces the Stable Flow Theory of Proofs (SFTP), a novel framework aimed at understanding and potentially harnessing the inherent stability within proof processes. The core concept of SFTP posits that proof development evolves through a series of intermediate states (P_t) which ultimately converge towards a stable state (P*). This convergence, while not always immediately apparent, represents a fundamental flow within the proof, and deviations from this flow can introduce instability and hinder successful completion. The theory suggests that understanding and manipulating this stable flow could provide a new theoretical foundation for automated theorem proving, moving beyond current approaches that often rely on exhaustive search or heuristics. The paper explores the implications of this theory, focusing on identifying and characterizing the factors influencing this stable flow, and ultimately, outlining a potential methodology for leveraging this stability to improve automated proof generation. ---

title: Self-Specialized Teachers for Domain Post-Training
abstract: Target-only post-training can improve performance in a specialized domain while degrading behaviors that a general-purpose base model acquired before adaptation. We study this problem when target-domain data are available but a representative replay corpus is not. We propose self-specialized teacher distillation (SSTD), a two-stage procedure that first trains a copy of the base model into a domain teacher, then distills its token distribution to a student on prefixes sampled from the student itself. Teacher training combines standard target supervision with base-aware key-token weighting and distribution alignment to the frozen base model; on-policy distillation then places domain feedback on states the student can encounter at inference time. On financial numerical reasoning, medical question answering, and legal holding identification, SSTD retains much of the target improvement of direct fine-tuning while improving the mean score on the evaluated general suite by 4.8--5.0 points at the reported operating point. The pattern persists across Qwen3 sizes and on Gemma backbones. SSTD requires neither an external teacher nor general replay data.

title: CoupVisor: Strategy Optimization by Round and Challenge Decision Support
abstract: This paper presents CoupVisor, a decision-support system for the hidden-information card game Coup. It addresses two questions: what a player should do on each turn, and when a player should challenge an opponent's claim. The system is built around a single description of game events, which is shared across manual play, replay of recorded games, simulation, belief tracking, advisor recommendations, and learning-based policies. title: A Study on a Food Pairing Knowledge Graph Construction Method Integrating Large Language Models and Relation Completion
abstract: Aiming at scattered knowledge sources, inconsistent entity expressions and insufficient relation extraction accuracy in food pairing, this paper proposes a food pairing knowledge graph construction method integrating large language models and relation completion. A domain ontology covering dishes, ingredients, nutrients, dietary restrictions, applicable populations and health goals is designed. Candidate entities and relations are then extracted from recipe texts, nutrition descriptions and dietary-restriction materials using a large language model, and entity normalization is performed through a domain dictionary and semantic embeddings. Finally, a relation scoring function integrating LLM confidence, semantic similarity and domain rules is used to filter, review and complete candidate triples. Experiments on a food pairing corpus show that the proposed method achieves a relation extraction F1 score of 88.71%, which is 6.05 percentage points higher than direct LLM extraction, and obtains a human-verified accuracy of 87.33% for completed relations. The results indicate that the proposed method can provide a reliable structured knowledge base for healthy diet recommendation and food pairing question answering.

title: Hierarchical Abstraction Cost: A Computability Analysis for Autonomous Agents
abstract: Hierarchical Abstraction Cost: A Computability Analysis for Autonomous Agents Bounded-optimality theory defines an intelligent agent as one that makes the best possible use of the computation its architecture provides, but it takes the action space over which that computation is exercised as given, and says nothing about how a long-horizon goal should first be broken into subgoals so that bounded computation is enough to solve it at all. This paper introduces Hierarchical Abstraction Cost (HAC), a family of measures that scores a state transition according to the abstraction level at which it is planned, derived purely from the transition structure of an environment rather than supplied by a designer or discovered by a task-specific heuristic. Five structural properties are proposed for a well-founded hierarchical difficulty measure, and established subgoal-discovery rules from the hierarchical reinforcement learning literature — betweenness centrality, empowerment, and graph-partition boundary states — are each shown to violate at least one. Building on HAC, hierarchical intelligence is split into two independent quantities, strategic competence and learning efficiency, and a separation theorem is proved: HAC is polynomial-time computable under a subgoal-count resource bias, but uncomputable in general under a program-length bias absent oracle access to the environment. A worked room-corridor example and a discussion of curriculum design, self-improvement limits, and alignment implications accompany the formal results. Keywords: hierarchical reinforcement learning, subgoal discovery, computability theory, bounded rationality, bounded optimality, autonomous agents, intrinsic reward, universal intelligence, Kolmogorov complexity, curriculum learning, AI alignment.

title: Computational Proof Dynamics Theory (CPDT)
abstract: Computational Proof Dynamics Theory (CPDT) introduces a novel framework for analyzing how proof strategies evolve over time within automated and semi‑automated reasoning systems. By formalizing the transition from a strategy at time t, denoted Strategy_t, to the next strategy Strategy_{t+1}, CPDT treats proof search as a discrete dynamical system that can be studied using tools from nonlinear dynamics, reinforcement learning, and information theory. The core idea is that proof strategies are not static; they adapt in response to the structure of the problem space, the feedback from intermediate proofs, and the computational resources available. This paper develops the mathematical underpinnings of CPDT, proposes an algorithmic architecture that implements dynamic strategy adaptation, and discusses the potential of CPDT to achieve breakthroughs in mathematical intelligence, including the prospect of contributing to the next Turing Award for foundational advances in automated reasoning. The work is organized into six sections: Introduction, Mathematical Foundations, Dynamic Model of Strategy Evolution, Algorithmic Framework, Applications and Future Work, and Conclusion.

title: Computational Personality Space Theory (CPST): A Mathematical Framework for Machine Personality Analysis
abstract: The rapid proliferation of intelligent systems has raised the fundamental question of how to quantify and compare their internal states in a principled way. Computational Personality Space Theory (CPST) proposes a comprehensive mathematical framework that encapsulates all possible computational personalities within a high‑dimensional space denoted by Omega_P. Each personality is represented as a vector of behavioral and cognitive attributes, and the theory introduces a well‑defined metric for measuring personality distances across heterogeneous intelligent systems. CPST bridges the gap between qualitative psychological concepts and quantitative machine learning constructs, providing a basis for cross‑system personality comparison, personality evolution tracking, and the design of adaptive human‑machine interaction protocols. The paper presents the theoretical underpinnings, formal definitions, and potential applications of CPST, arguing that this approach could form the foundation for a new generation of machine personality research with implications for AI safety, explainability, and user experience design.

title: How Language Models Choose Sides: Internal Representations of Instruction Hierarchy
abstract: We study how instruction-tuned LLMs arbitrate direct conflicts between system and user instructions. We introduce a benchmark of 41 paired constraints with deterministic verifiers and evaluate eight models under matched baseline, conflict, and same-channel control conditions. Behaviourally, the models split into three regimes by System Authority Delta: hierarchy-respecting models use the system channel as an authority signal, anti-hierarchy models follow the system less often than their same-channel baseline predicts, and no-effect models show little channel sensitivity. Llama-3.1-8B is the strongest anti-hierarchy case in our suite, following the system in only 0.10 of conflict trials. We use this behavioural failure case to ask whether user-preferring arbitration reflects the absence of an internal conflictresolution signal. It does not: on Llama-3.1-8B, the conflict outcome is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations at 0.97 balanced accuracy, 17 percentage points above a metadata-only baseline, with analogous signals on Qwen2.5-7B and gpt-oss-20b. Steering with a layer-12 mean of four per-conflict logistic-regression directions raises genuine system compliance from 0.132 to 0.530, while directions selected mainly for pooled separability steer poorly. User-preferring conflict resolution can therefore coexist with a readable internal arbitration signal, and successful intervention depends on the geometry of the readout rather than probe accuracy alone

title: Inclinations! — A road to the Singularity
abstract: Inclinations! — A road to the Singularity presents PEDLER as a foundational transition calculus in which configurations and states are connected by transitions, an inclination is the directional primitive associated with a transition, an inclination field is the resulting structure of inclinations over transitions, and a Walk is the realised trajectory through configuration space. The work extends these primitives through competition of inclinations, lateral inhibition, state spawning, PEDLER semantics, signals and systems, and proposed correlations with wave–particle duality, collapse, and configuration geometry as a possible route toward spacetime geometry and gravity. It further applies the transition-field framework to chemistry, biochemistry, genetics and evolution. The book describes physical and computational realizations through NI2A2 and the physical-AI lineage, CEMs as synthetiform realization, CEMb as bioform realization and neural decoding, LVF and ILM as linguistic architectures, and Eco-CEM as an ecological realization path. CEMs includes conventional AI acceleration and proposed neuromorphic and quantum-neuromorphic realization; CEMb includes neural observation, decoding and semantic cognitive-state recovery. Quantum Neuromorphic BCI is described as a proposed bidirectional bridge between CEMb and CEMs, with shared semantic structure, Intent, refinement and verified equivalence providing the convergence architecture. The work also presents the historical physical-AI corpus, physical laboratory realization, the CEM family and its symmetry, Intent middleware, the Unified Ecosystem Architecture, and Interpretive Working Basis Theory. The proposed Singularity is treated as convergence of bioform and synthetiform cognition rather than as an established physical event. Cross-domain statements identified as hypotheses or correlations retain that status; the work does not silently promote proposed correspondences in neuroscience, quantum physics, gravity, biology or computation to established findings.

title: Computational Causal Explanation Theory (CCET): A New Paradigm for AI Explanation
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems have traditionally focused on producing accurate predictions or decisions. The resulting outputs, however, rarely provide insight into the underlying causes that led to a particular result. This paper introduces the Computational Causal Explanation Theory (CCET), a formal framework that augments standard AI outputs with rigorous causal explanations. CCET unifies the concepts of structural causal models, counterfactual reasoning, and deterministic mappings to produce a joint output consisting of the predicted value and its causal justification. The theory is presented in a purely mathematical form, with all symbols expressed in plain text to facilitate direct transcription. CCET's core contribution lies in demonstrating that any AI system can be re‑engineered to compute not only "what" but also "why", thereby redefining interpretability and accountability in machine learning. The potential impact of CCET extends to safety‑critical domains, regulatory compliance, and the broader scientific community, offering a path toward systems that can explain their reasoning in a manner comparable to human experts.

title: A hybrid hierarchical multimodal learning with autoencoders, vision transformers and deep belief networks for liver cancer detection
abstract: A clinical problem of early liver cancer is one of the most urgent ones due to the insidious nature of tumors, the lack of multimodal data consistency and large inter-subject variation. Conventional systems of diagnosing rely highly on manual interpretation and monomodality images that typically result in delayed diagnosis and reduced effectiveness in the treatment. The researcher in this study presents another model of multimodal deep intelligence to detect and categorize early liver cancer through the combination of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) data. The provided solution is an integrated self-regularized autoencoder (AE) to learn the multimodal representation and allows noise suppression and compression of latent features. Vision Transformer (ViT) involves extracting long-range spatial dependencies and context in fused representations. Dynamic maximization of diagnostic decision policy and classification confidence under different clinical settings ML networks are A Deep Belief Network (DBN) that has hierarchical tissue abstraction and probabilistic pattern modelling and Deep Q-Network (DQN) that optimizes diagnostic decision policy and classification confidence. A standard liver imaging dataset (612 institutional patients to be assessed in the first instance and 512 public patients to be assessed in the second instance) yields high diagnostic quality, potential for generalization, and classification accuracy with positive results of 98.76% (95% CI 98.12–99.34) and an AUC of 0.992 (95% The findings confirm that there was successful multimodal fusion with heterogeneous deep learning paradigms in the detection of early liver cancer. This research will add the presence of scalable, intelligent, and clinically relevant diagnostic architecture to facilitate timely responses and decision support systems to manage liver cancer.

title: Amortised Post-Hoc Explanation with Exact Preservation for Dynamic Graph Anomaly Detectors
abstract: Anomaly detection in dynamic graphs underpins financial fraud analysis, intrusion detection, and platform integrity, where automated decisions require human-interpretable justifications. StrGNN, the strongest performer in recent benchmarks, produces no explanation: when an edge is flagged, the analyst receives only a score. Explanation metrics are undefined for StrGNN because no attribution vector exists. This paper closes that gap. We present X-StrGNN, a post-hoc explanation layer that wraps a trained, frozen StrGNN and emits, for every flagged edge, dual attributions: a structural attribution identifying which contextual interactions in the enclosing subgraph drove the decision, and a temporal attribution identifying which historical snapshot carried the signal. Both attributions are multiplicative masks identically one in the unexplained pass, so the layer is an exact pass-through: detection is preserved to machine precision, verified rather than asserted (Delta AUC = 0.0000, Delta AP = 0.0000, Delta P@100 = 0.0000). Attribution costs 0.66 ms per edge, making explanation of an entire alarm list feasible. We conduct the first controlled design study of attribution strategies for this architecture, comparing gradient attribution, per-instance mask optimisation, and amortised parameterisation under one protocol, one budget, and three seeds. X-StrGNN attains the highest stability (0.913) at 268x lower cost than per-instance optimisation, and its temporal attribution (1.601 against a measured random floor of 0.973) is separably better than its ablated control, while per-instance optimisation - the most expensive strategy - falls below that floor. Code, protocol, and per-seed measurements are released.

title: Symmetric Folding Principle for Quantum Propagator Synthesis
abstract: We introduce the symmetric-folding principle, a geometric quantum-control framework that lifts quantum state steering to exact propagator synthesis. The required structure is a folding symmetry: a unitary transformation that reverses the drift Hamiltonian while preserving the admissible control space. The method recasts propagator synthesis on the unitary group as steering of a chosen quantum state variable between fibers of an equivariant quotient map, followed by a prescribed folded continuation of the controls. We prove that control inputs satisfying the resulting fiber-transfer condition, when extended by the prescribed folded continuation, generate the desired unitary propagator in the associated symmetry-selected target family. This gives two key structural advantages. The fiber-transfer condition constrains the midpoint propagator only to a coset of the folding symmetry's centralizer. The prescribed fold cancels this residual freedom exactly. Thus a full group-level endpoint constraint is replaced by a lower-codimension fiber/coset condition, giving additional freedom in control design. For quantum ensembles, different members may reach different midpoint propagators within the same coset, while the folded sequence still yields a common final propagator for all ensemble members. This parameter-dependent freedom can be especially significant for robust ensemble-propagator design. We demonstrate the construction on an SO(3) Bloch ensemble and an SU (4) scalar-coupled two-spin system.

title: Memory That Doesn't Expire: Agentic Long-Term Memory for Conversational Agents on a Single Consumer GPU
abstract: Conversational agents forget: once a dialogue outgrows the context window, a model must either be reminded through retrieval or have its history truncated. Recent memory systems address this with extraction and retrieval, but they assume a large, often API-hosted model as the memory manager, an assumption that rules out private, local deployment. We ask whether a small local model, on a single consumer GPU, can manage long-term memory well, and how the answer depends on model size. We evaluate four memory strategies (no memory, full-history stuffing, raw-turn retrieval, and an agentic protocol that extracts typed, dated, deduplicated facts) on LoCoMo (1,986 questions over 10 long multi-session conversations), scored by an independent LLM judge. Full-context stuffing wins aggregate accuracy when the answer still lies inside the window, but its advantage is an artifact of conversation length: split by whether a question's evidence survives truncation, stuffing collapses by 76% beyond the window while agentic memory stays flat, outperforming stuffing 2.0x on the 39% of questions that already exceed it. Agentic memory further gives the best temporal reasoning of any strategy (via absolute-date grounding at write time) using ~67x less context. Varying the extractor from 3B to 14B, we find quality scales with size and that temporal grounding is the first capability to break under compression, setting a minimum viable memory-manager size of ~7-14B, comfortably within a 12 GB GPU. A hand-verified audit of 200 stored memories finds 199 faithful to their source turn, with no fabrications. We release the system, the benchmark harness, and the raw judged outputs behind every reported number. title: Confident but Incorrect: Measuring LLM Confidence Calibration for Mathematical Problem-Solving
abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly being used as tools for mathematical problem-solving and have shown progressive improvement in reasoning capability. However, even frontier LLMs remain prone to hallucination when challenged with problems beyond their capabilities, often presenting incorrect reasoning with high confidence. In this paper, we examine how LLM self-assessed confidence aligns with empirical accuracy across math problems of varying difficulty and type. Furthermore, we test a model’s confidence on both its initial attempt and a prompted retry in which the model is informed of its prior error. Our method reveals a systematic overestimation of confidence that persists even after the model is informed of prior error, with miscalibration increasing largely monotonically with problem difficulty. These findings highlight the gap between perceived and actual LLM reliability in mathematical reasoning.
